source.title: Blind Single-Layer Activation Edits Show a Break/Fix Asymmetry in Factual Recall

record.file_problem: The full paper is present; no apparent garbling or cutoff.
record.tranche_reason: Uses SAE features and a feature-overlap hypothesis as tools for studying factual-error detection and repair. Its results evaluate the paper’s CIS-based approach, not whether superposition’s geometry or capacity account holds.
record.gate_note: The paper mentions superposition as background and tests whether SAE feature overlap (CIS) predicts or enables factual repair. Those experiments do not test the listed versions’ claims about toy-model geometry, capacity-driven polysemanticity, feature recoverability as canonical units, or dimensionality of features. SAE and CIS outcomes are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The paper cites superposition as background and uses SAE features and a feature-overlap score (CIS) as tools to predict and repair factual errors in Pythia-6.9B. Its results measure hallucination prediction and repair performance, not whether features are superposed, why neurons are polysemantic, or whether SAE features are canonical or one-dimensional. The overlap numbers (Jaccard) describe SAE feature-set overlap that depends on SAE type. They are not a measure of superposition in the model.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct but incomplete. The paper's main conclusion is a break/fix asymmetry: single-layer activation edits corrupt 74–100% of correct answers across three models, while blind repair yields at most +3 pp net. Oracle ablations point to a bottleneck in selecting the target-specific direction. The CIS/SAE part is a secondary negative result: a weak signal (AUROC 0.58) that vanishes under Top-K SAEs, and suppression with zero effect. The authors read this as consistent with polysemantic co-activation rather than genuine interference.
record.recipe_differences: Uses trained L1 and Top-K SAEs and a CIS-based prediction/suppression procedure; it does not reproduce the toy-model method or test its representational geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: CIS prediction differs between L1, native Top-K, and post-hoc sparsified L1 representations; the tested Top-K values are k ∈ {32, 64, 128}.

fits_no_version.finding: Concept feature-set overlap differs strongly by SAE type: L1 SAE Jaccard 0.269 vs Top-K 0.032 on the same layer. CIS predicts hallucination weakly with L1 (AUROC 0.58) and at chance with Top-K or post-hoc sparsification (0.42–0.50).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Apparent feature overlap between concepts in SAE representations depends on the SAE sparsity regime (L1 vs Top-K), so dense L1 overlap may reflect co-activation artefacts rather than model-level feature interference.

fits_no_version.finding: Reconstructing activations through the L1 SAE preserves hallucination-probe AUROC (.896, r=.9996).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: L1 SAE reconstruction at layer 24 of Pythia-6.9B retains the linearly decodable hallucination signal.

fits_no_version.finding: CIS-guided suppression of competitor features changes accuracy by zero (p>0.99), and SAE feature exchange changes it by at most 1.4 pp. Zeroing entity-specific SAE features flips 100% of correct answers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE feature-level interventions break factual recall easily but do not repair factual errors in this setting.

record.code_released: Code for SAEs, CIS, and intervention experiments will be released; URL not stated.
record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 4th Workshop on Towards Knowledgeable Foundation Models (KnowFM 2026)
record.problems: The SAE/CIS results concern an indirect representation and one tested intervention, not direct measurements of model-feature geometry. The authors note that the SAE feature-suppression procedure is conservative and that other feature-level interventions were not tested. Several related evaluations use small pools.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant numerical SAE/CIS results were identified for extraction.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, no sparsity transition, no geometry.
All: no capacity or importance analysis.
All. The authors attribute the CIS signal to 'polysemantic co-activation', but they do not test what causes polysemanticity.
All. SAEs are trained and reconstruction preserves probe AUROC, but recovery of sparse model features is not evaluated as such.
All. The L1 vs Top-K overlap difference shows SAE-dependence of feature sets, but completeness, stability and canonicity are not tested.

record.verdict_notes: Superposition appears only as the motivating hypothesis. The study is one of the original source's citers, not a test of it. No verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-model superposition, overlapping near-orthogonal directions, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether polysemanticity results from competition for limited representational capacity or importance-based dimension allocation.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.
Whether real-model features are spread across neurons or whether SAEs recover the model’s features.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units of model representation.
Whether represented features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional.
